newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Battered regionals face more losses.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Battered regionals face more losses.

text.p: Regional currencies remained vulnerable to further losses in late Thursday trade after plumbing new depths on stop-loss selling.
What began as a speculative attack on Southeast Asian currencies had turned into a rush to hedge, analysts said.

"It's a brave man who speculates in these markets now," said Tim Lucas, treasury manager at Bank of Bermuda in Hong Kong. "What's happening now is genuine portfolio hedging and genuine concern as opposed to having a speculative play."
The Thai baht, which led the decline, recovered from its lows of around 32.70 to the dollar but continued to look depressed against a backdrop of financial sector woes.
Of 18 finance and securities firms reporting half year figures, only seven made a profit and the sector's losses as a whole totalled a depressing 3.5 billion baht (US$108 million).
There was talk the central Bank of Thailand (BOT) had intervened to sell dollars above the 32.60 baht level, helping the baht stage a mild recovery.
A BOT official declined to confirm or deny the market talk, saying only that the central bank was "monitoring the market closely".
The baht was at 31.950/32.020 to the dollar onshore at 0955 GMT and 31.930/32.030 offshore.
Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said he would announce a major economic package within two weeks that would help stabilise the baht and bring down Thai interest rates.
The relatively resilient Singapore dollar caved in to mounting pressure, falling through the psychological 1.47 level against the U.S. dollar on stop-loss sales.
Dealers attributed Thursday's sharp drop to Finance Minister Richard Hu's comments about Singapore's competitiveness not being hurt by the recent tumble of other Southeast Asian currencies.
Hu told parliament on Wednesday Singapore's exchange rate was determined by market demand and it would continue to be managed on a trade-weighted basis with a medium-term perspective.
The Singapore dollar fell to a 32-month low of 1.4785 and was quoted at 1.4770/75 at 1000 GMT.
"It was mainly interbank stop-losses being triggered and we've broken out of all the highs for the last few years," said the regional currency chief at a European bank.
He said the U.S. dollar was gearing up for a move towards S$1.50 and could reach that level within a month if regional turmoil persisted.

In Malaysia, the ringgit remained depressed after crashing to an early low of 2.6540 to the dollar on spillover weakness. Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's call for cooperation among Southeast Asian countries to fight against currency speculation gave the market brief pause, dealers said.
But the ringgit soon succumbed to selling again as players shrugged the comments off as simply a suggestion.
The European bank dealer said Kuala Lumpur banks had sold the dollar near its highs, raising the spectre of Bank Negara intervention.
"But that may be just for corporate interests because normally when they intervene, they use their own name," he said.
The Indonesian rupiah was back below the 2,600 level to the dollar in late trade but its decline was relatively muted, partly due to signs the central bank had been intervened.
"They came in above the 2,610 level once and around the 2,600 level later but generally the market strategy is still to buy the dollar on any dips," a dealer said.
"The rupiah is moving in a steady mode compared to the rest. So they're not that alarmed. I think they're just trying to smooth the flow," he added.
The rupiah was at 2,613/23 against an opening at 2,575/85.
The Philippine peso ended steady at 28.500/550 to the dollar against its previous 28.5.
Hong Kong dollar forwards remained near their highs despite talk of heavy intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.
Three-month currency forwards were at 320/350 and six-months at 560/610 against Wednesday's levels of 130 and 170 respectively.
Dealers said funds were buying the U.S. dollar forward, anticipating a fall in the Hong Kong dollar, which is pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar.

-- Madhav Reddy in Kuala Lumpur (603-206 2323), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221 384-6364), Anchalee Koetsawang in Bangkok (662) 652-0642, Lilian Karunungan in Manila (632-841-8937), Sarah Davison in Hong Kong (852-2843-6470) and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703090) (c) Reuters Limited 1997
